Workers End Strike at Major Chinese Cement Producers, Operations Resume

A week-long strike by thousands of workers at major cement plants in China’s Shandong province has concluded after management and labor representatives reached an agreement on salary adjustments and working conditions. The work stoppage, which began last Monday, disrupted production at several facilities operated by industry leaders such as Eastern Materials Group and Shandong United Cement, leading to a temporary reduction in output in one of the country’s key construction materials regions.

According to the Shandong Construction Materials Trade Union, the strike was triggered by workers’ demands for a 10% wage increase and improvements to overtime policies. “Our members have long contributed to the growth of this vital industry, and it was important their voices were heard,” said union official Li Chengyu. “The agreement provides an 8% wage increase and a commitment from management to review scheduling practices.”

Production lines were halted at five major plants in Zibo and Jinan, with an estimated daily output loss of over 20,000 tons, according to figures provided by the Shandong Construction Materials Association. The disruption led to concerns among local contractors about potential delays in ongoing infrastructure projects.

Analysts say the labor dispute highlights mounting pressure within the industry as input costs rise and the workforce becomes more vocal about working conditions. “This incident underscores the need for ongoing dialogue between management and labor as the industry adapts to new economic realities,” said Zhao Weimin, a senior analyst at Capital Insight Partners in Beijing.

Operations resumed at all affected plants on Wednesday morning, with companies reporting that deliveries to customers were being prioritized to clear pending orders. A spokesperson for Eastern Materials Group confirmed, “We are working to restore supply chains and ensure that project timelines are met.”

Industry observers expect production to return to normal levels within the next week, but caution that further unrest could re-emerge if structural issues are not addressed.
